cards.title: Flag waving for Americans
cards.publisher: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service — Insects in the City
cards.lesson: Ensign wasps lay eggs inside cockroach egg cases, where their young feed on the roach eggs. Explain what this small, non-stinging visitor is doing in a home and how it attacks a hidden stage of the cockroach life cycle.
cards.species: Ensign wasp (Evania appendigaster); American cockroach (Periplaneta americana), with smokybrown and Oriental cockroaches also discussed
cards.region: Texas extension education; general biology relevant where the named cockroaches and wasps occur
cards.limits: An older educational article, not a Central Texas population survey. A wasp sighting is a clue, not proof of an active infestation or complete cockroach control. Do not extend the host relationship to every cockroach species.

facts.statement: A female ensign wasp places a single egg inside a cockroach egg case.
The developing wasp larva feeds on cockroach eggs inside that case.
facts.quote: wasp larva matures while feeding on the dozen or more cockroach eggs

facts.statement: The ensign wasp described in this article does not sting or bite people.
facts.quote: it does not sting or bite

cards.title: Why do I have roaches in my home?
cards.publisher: National Pesticide Information Center, Oregon State University
cards.lesson: Cockroaches can hitchhike indoors and survive even in well-kept homes. Explain why a sighting does not, by itself, mean poor housekeeping, and how incoming bags and containers can bring them inside.
cards.species: Household cockroaches; the article does not assign every entry route to one species
cards.region: General United States homeowner guidance; applicable entry routes are not a Central Texas prevalence estimate
cards.limits: This does not mean sanitation is unimportant or that a particular home's infestation came from a bag. Identify the species and inspect actual conditions before deciding the source. Exclude medical and pesticide-use sections from narration.

facts.statement: Finding cockroaches alone does not establish that a home is dirty.
facts.quote: Finding roaches is not a sign that your house is dirty.

facts.statement: Cockroaches can enter homes on bags, backpacks, suitcases and other containers.
facts.quote: Hitching a ride on bags, backpacks, suitcases and other containers.

cards.title: Cockroaches
cards.publisher: National Pesticide Information Center, Oregon State University
cards.lesson: Cockroaches are attracted to their own debris. Explain why cleanup includes dead roaches, eggs and droppings, and how sticky traps help reveal areas of activity.
cards.species: Household cockroaches; German and American cockroaches are discussed separately where their needs differ
cards.region: General United States guidance; no local infestation rates or Texas-specific measurements
cards.limits: The page states attraction to debris but does not explain the chemical mechanism or quantify the effect. Supporting science is needed for that depth. Traps monitor activity; this source does not establish that trapping or cleaning alone eliminates an infestation. Exclude medical and product-specific advice.

facts.statement: Cockroaches are attracted to their own debris, which the page identifies as dead cockroaches, eggs and feces.
facts.quote: Cockroaches are attracted to their own debris.

facts.statement: Sticky traps or glue boards can help identify areas of cockroach activity in a home.
facts.quote: Monitor and assess cockroach activity using sticky traps or glue boards.

cards.title: The Turkestan Cockroach: An Emerging Pest in Texas
cards.publisher: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service — Insects in the City
cards.lesson: Male and female Turkestan cockroaches can look like different species. Learn why the male's long wings and the female's shorter wings matter when identifying this Texas invader.
cards.species: Turkestan cockroach (Blatta lateralis); American and Oriental cockroaches appear as identification comparisons
cards.region: Texas reports include El Paso and North Texas; no claim of confirmed New Braunfels prevalence
cards.limits: The 2024 article is not a current distribution survey. Do not identify an unseen insect, imply every flying roach is Turkestan, or repeat its broad disease and water-contamination claims. Preserve the distinction between males, females and nymphs.

facts.statement: Adult male Turkestan cockroaches are slender and brownish orange/red, with long yellowish wings.
facts.quote: brownish orange/red, slender, and have long, yellowish wings

facts.statement: Adult female Turkestan cockroaches are broader than males and have short vestigial wings.
facts.quote: They are broader than Turkestan males and have short vestigial wings.

cards.title: Bug bombs bomb
cards.publisher: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service — Insects in the City
cards.lesson: An apartment study found no significant drop in German cockroach numbers after fogging. Explore why filling a room with insecticide fog does not guarantee reaching roaches in protected cracks.
cards.region: United States study summarized by Texas extension; researchers were at North Carolina State University, but this article does not specify the apartment locations
cards.limits: The findings concern the studied apartments, products and two-to-four-week follow-up, not every roach species or every treatment. The article discusses hiding and resistance; do not claim hiding alone caused the study result. Keep this a behavior and evidence lesson, without product recommendations, dosing or health advice.

facts.statement: In the apartment study summarized here, fogger-treated homes showed no significant decrease in free-roaming German cockroach numbers two to four weeks later.
facts.quote: there was no significant drop in these wild cockroach numbers

facts.statement: The extension article explains that cockroaches can retreat to protected crevices when they sense an irritating insecticide.
facts.quote: cockroaches typically hide in protective crevices when they sense an irritating insecticide
